reason: Even with classical Scott analysis of well orders and finite-condensation definability supplied, the task still requires a constructed sharp-complexity witness: a marked sum of two different rational shuffles, an explicit two-extra-round back-and-forth strategy, and orbit formulas that distinguish the first and second omega^lambda blocks while keeping the upper complexity at the claimed level. Both upper and lower obligations remain in the solution. This is beyond a routine qualifying-exam application of the Scott hierarchy. I support H2 for this specific construction; I do not count the much larger classification or Friedman–Stanley analysis elsewhere in the paper.
core_assessment:
two_round_shuffle_core: 1024–1056 was read in full. First answer copies the tuple in the initial A and final B, leaving only the interval spanning the inserted L unmatched and reversing the comparison for the next turn. Shuffle tails reduce that interval to A+L+B versus A+B. The second response maps L+B into a final segment of B=L·Q; its remaining unmatched gap reduces, after removing common end pieces, to A<=_alpha A+B. The shuffle identity A≅A+A and the original A<=_alpha B finish. The two extra rounds are proved, not assumed.
construction_and_nonisomorphism: 1530–1533 uses L1=1+Z+omega^lambda, L2=1+Z+omega^lambda·2, A=L1·Q, B=L2·Q and L=A+L2+B. Isolated finite-condensation singleton markers delimit the relevant blocks. L has a least doubled-ordinal block, while A+B has doubled blocks but no least one, so they are not isomorphic.
upper_orbit_bound: 1534–1560: pt, Z, init and gamma positions distinguish the singleton marker, integer chain and points in the first well-order copy. The additional sec predicate uses all lower finite-condensation relations and has complexity Pi_lambda; gamma2 has complexity Sigma_(lambda+1). Finite tuple orbits further record their order, same-block relationships and finite differences within a Z copy. These are within the stated bound. Naming the marker in the distinguished central L2 separates the three pieces and gives the parameterized orbit bound needed by the explicitly allowed Scott-sentence criterion.
lower_complexity_bound: The classical well-order comparison gives L1<=_(lambda+1)L2 and hence the corresponding shuffle comparison A<=_(lambda+1)B. Applying the fully proved shuffle lemma and its lower-bound corollary gives a nonisomorphic comparison at lambda+3, ruling out Pi_(lambda+3). Together with the Sigma_(lambda+3) upper bound this supplies the exact claimed sentence complexity.
prerequisite_assessment: The named-parameter Scott criterion, interval back-and-forth criterion, well-order comparison and Sigma_(2*delta) finite-condensation definability are appropriately explicit standard inputs. They do not supply the shuffle witness or the two-round strategy. For a nonzero countable limit lambda, each finite lower-level predicate and each gamma<omega^lambda interval type used in the first copy has complexity below lambda; the countable conjunction defining sec reaches Pi_lambda and one existential layer gives Sigma_(lambda+1). The problem explicitly restricts the ordinal scope to countable nonzero limits, as required.

The subsequent gamma2 formula uses precisely that interpretation.

issues.finding: The gamma-position descriptions are read as forward intervals from the indicated initial point. At gamma=0 this means the initial point itself, already separately defined by init or sec; it is not an assertion that every point preceding an initial point has rank0 because a backwards set interval is empty. This is the positional meaning expressly stated by the author.

standard_prerequisites.name: Infinitary Scott analysis and back-and-forth preservation
standard_prerequisites.statement: A Sigma-in_alpha formula is an infinitary countable disjunction of existential blocks over lower-level Pi formulas, with the dual definition for Pi. The back-and-forth preorder matches those formula classes. If all tuple orbits are Sigma-in_alpha definable over a fixed finite tuple, a Sigma-in_(alpha+2) Scott sentence exists. A nonisomorphic K with L<=_beta K rules out a Pi-in_beta Scott sentence of L.
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Source45-86 and the stated standard background173-184.
standard_prerequisites.use: Translate the actual orbit upper bounds and constructed nonisomorphic back-and-forth witness into exact sentence complexity.

standard_prerequisites.name: Classical Scott analysis of well orders and finite condensation
standard_prerequisites.statement: For a nonzero countable limit ordinal lambda, omega^lambda <=_(lambda+1) omega^lambda*2. For each gamma<omega^lambda its interval isomorphism type has infinitary complexity below lambda. The finite-condensation relations start with equality, take finite distance in the quotient at successors, and take unions at limits; relation sim_delta is Sigma-in_(2*delta) definable.
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Source1314-1333,1381-1391 and1530-1544; Ash1986, Ash-Knight2000 and Alvir-Rossegger2020.
standard_prerequisites.use: Only the well-order building blocks and definability of block relations are allowed. The shuffle-sum construction, orbit definitions and two-round back-and-forth argument are not assumed.

core_obligations: Prove the shuffle-sum lemma that inserting a distinguished L block costs two rounds in the asymmetric back-and-forth comparison.
Construct the two dense sums with blocks 1+Z+omega^lambda and 1+Z+omega^lambda*2, then insert one distinguished block at their interface.
Define singleton finite blocks, Z positions, first ordinal positions and second ordinal positions by the displayed infinitary formulas, with the required quantifier-complexity bounds.
Recover tuple orbits over the distinguished interface point and prove the upper Scott-sentence bound.
Use the two-round lemma and a genuinely nonisomorphic order obtained by removing the first doubled block to prove no Pi-in_(lambda+3) Scott sentence exists.

proof_roadmap.step: Two-stage interval strategy: first copy the initial and terminal shuffle sums, then absorb the distinguished block into a final segment; reduce the only nonisomorphic interval to the given alpha-comparison.
Construct L1,L2,A,B,L and define orbits in the one-ordinal blocks.
Define second-copy initial points using all lower finite-condensation relations, then all remaining positions with one additional alternation.
Apply the fully supplied shuffle lemma for the matching lower bound.

approved_task_config.difficulty_reason: Even after standard Scott analysis of well orders is allowed, the task must combine a bespoke two-round shuffle-sum comparison with an explicit transfinite orbit-definability construction. The upper and lower bounds involve different mechanisms: locating the second omega^lambda copy by all lower condensation relations, and concealing an inserted distinguished block from a long back-and-forth game. It is not just calculating the rank of a given ordinal. The precise H2/H3 boundary remains for independent review.

compared.difference: The public primary is the back-and-forth behavior of powers of Z. This target is a dense mixed-block order of exact Sigma-in_(lambda+3) complexity; its proof does not use the published timesZ lemma.

compared.difference: This construction is non-scattered (it contains Q); the cited scattered-order tools only supply standard well-order facts. Final exact-claim comparison still needed.

The formula is preserved; this variable-description slip is explicitly recorded for independent review.

The upper-bound passage uses the standard named-parameter Scott-rank criterion stated among the inputs. The lower-bound comparison is with A+B; it is not isomorphic to A+L2+B because the latter has a least doubled-ordinal block and the former does not.
